frames.narration: A user uploads a photo. The upload service stores the file privately, so nobody can see it yet, and starts the checks. The first check is the cheapest.

The service computes an exact hash and a perceptual hash and looks both up in the known-bad index in memory. There is no exact match, and the nearest stored perceptual hash is 19 bits away, far above the limit of 6, so it is not a copy of anything known. This takes 4 ms.

Next the classifiers score the image for each kind of harm. The highest is 'hate symbol' at 0.62. This category has a high threshold of 0.95 for automatic removal and a low threshold of 0.20 for automatic approval, so 0.62 falls in the band that needs a person.

The item goes into the review queue with a priority built from the category, the score and the audience of the poster. Its deadline is 24 hours, because the score is mid-range and the account is small. Meanwhile the photo stays held, so the user sees 'being checked'.

A reviewer who works on this category pulls the highest priority item. The queue locks it to this reviewer. The image is shown blurred, and they open the full size, see that it is a banned symbol in a news context, and label it.

The decision service looks up the label in policy version 41, region by region. In most countries news context is allowed with an age gate, in Germany it is hidden, so the photo is published everywhere and hidden in one place. The service has stored one decision for this item id, so a retry would not repeat it.

The decision is appended to the log with the content id, the label, the classifier version and score, the policy version, the reviewer and the time. The uploader is notified that a restriction applies in one country, with the reason and an appeal link.

The uploader appeals. The appeal is a new item in the same queue and goes to a different reviewer. That reviewer agrees with the label, so the decision stands and the log records the appeal as 'upheld'. If it had been overturned, the content would be restored and the first decision marked as an error, and that count is what measures the real error rate.
